## Assessment (what is built)

A single Next.js App Router application (`apps/web`, Next 15.5.14 resolved, React 19) carries the entire product: marketing site, member surfaces, admin surfaces, platform admin, and all backend logic as route handlers under `src/app/api`. Worth stating plainly: despite the project description mentioning a Hono API, there is no Hono app in this repo. `apps/` contains only `web`, and all API traffic goes through Next route handlers wrapped by `src/lib/api.ts`. That is a fine architecture for this stage, but the mental model should match the code.

Coverage against the contract, item by item:

1. **App Router structure and routing conventions.** Clean and conventional. Tenant scoping via `/t/[slug]/...` for pages mirrored by `/api/v1/t/[slug]/...` for handlers is a tidy, predictable convention (`src/app/t/[slug]/admin`, `src/app/api/v1/t/[slug]/requests/...`). Route groups are not used, but with only three surface families (platform admin, tenant admin, tenant member) the flat structure holds. Assessed, no structural issue. One nit: `src/middleware.ts` declares `PROTECTED_PATHS = ["/t/"]` at line 6 and never uses it; the middleware only cookie-gates paths containing `/dashboard` (line 18), so admin page protection rests entirely on the server layouts, which do the job properly (`src/app/t/[slug]/admin/layout.tsx:23-29`).

2. **Server/client boundary discipline.** Mixed. 63 of ~100 `.tsx` files are `"use client"`, and 19 of 33 `page.tsx` files are full client components. The high-value detail pages (requests queue, request detail, member detail, fob detail, member dashboard) are server components that fetch via Drizzle inline, which is the right call. But sibling list pages (`admin/members/page.tsx`, `admin/fobs/page.tsx`, all of `admin/config/*`) are wholly client-rendered. See F-4. `src/components/auth-provider.tsx` is a five-line client component that renders `<>{children}</>`, a vestigial wrapper that forces nothing today but is dead weight in the root layout.

3. **Data-fetching patterns.** Two idioms coexist: server components querying Drizzle directly inside `withTenant` transactions (good, e.g. `src/app/t/[slug]/admin/page.tsx:38-70`), and client pages doing bare `fetch("/api/v1/t/...")` in `useEffect` with hand-rolled debounce and pagination (92 `fetch(` call sites in page/component code). No caching layer, no SWR/React Query, no request deduplication. See F-4.

4. **State management.** Local `useState` only. No global store, no context beyond the vestigial AuthProvider. For this product's shape (page-scoped CRUD) that is a defensible choice and I would not add Redux/Zustand. The cost shows up only in the giant forms (F-8), not in the absence of a store. Assessed, no issue with the approach itself.

5. **Component library usage.** Genuinely consistent. A single shadcn-style kit in `src/components/ui/` wraps `@base-ui/react` primitives (`ui/select.tsx`, `ui/dialog.tsx`, `ui/drawer.tsx` over vaul), with `class-variance-authority` variants and shared `button-variants.ts`. Every page I sampled uses the same Card/Button/Input/Select/Badge vocabulary. This is a strength (S-4).

6. **Form handling and client-side validation.** Hand-rolled. Zod is a dependency and is used in API routes, but no client form validates against a schema; validation is ad-hoc `disabled=` gating and server round-trips (`src/app/t/[slug]/request/request-form.tsx:566,1026,1111`). The 1,117-line request wizard is the pressure point. See F-8.

7. **Error handling and error boundaries.** The single biggest structural gap. There is not one `error.tsx`, `global-error.tsx`, or `not-found.tsx` in the entire app (verified by exhaustive find). See F-3. Client fetch errors are handled per-call, sometimes well (payment page), sometimes swallowed silently with `.catch(() => {})` (7 occurrences, e.g. the stats fetch at `src/app/t/[slug]/admin/members/page.tsx:108-116`, where a failed stats call just renders no stats with no signal to user or Sentry).

8. **Loading/suspense/skeleton states.** Good on the server-rendered admin routes: 11 `loading.tsx` files backed by a shared, well-built `src/components/loading-skeleton.tsx` (PageSkeleton/DetailSkeleton). `Suspense` correctly wraps `useSearchParams` consumers (`src/app/sign-in/page.tsx:42`). Client-fetching pages manage their own loading flags adequately. Assessed, minor inconsistency only (client list pages show text spinners rather than the skeleton kit).

9. **Accessibility.** Middling. The base-ui primitives carry solid keyboard and ARIA behaviour for free, inputs get real `<Label htmlFor>`, and `queue-item.tsx:431` shows deliberate care (`aria-label` on the mobile full-card tap target with the text link kept in a higher stacking context). But there is zero `aria-live`/`role="alert"` anywhere and no programmatic focus management (grep confirms no `focus()` calls), so async error messages in the sign-in form and request wizard are invisible to screen readers, and the multi-step wizard leaves focus stranded between steps. Contrast of the status chips (`text-green-700` on `bg-green-50` etc., `admin/members/page.tsx:44-55`) passes at the sizes used. See F-10.

10. **Responsive/mobile behaviour.** A clear strength. The mobile admin bottom-sheet nav (`src/components/mobile-admin-nav.tsx`) carries a belt-and-braces route-change close effect with a comment documenting the exact production failure it prevents (captured scroll-lock making the whole PWA feel dead). Queue rows re-layout to two rows on mobile with a full-card tap target. The PWA layer (manifest, icons, standalone detection in `sign-in-form.tsx:12-16` switching magic-link to OTP because magic links break in standalone mode) shows real device-tested judgement.

11. **Bundle size and client payload.** Better than the dependency list suggests. Every scary dependency is server-only, verified: `xlsx` only in `src/lib/services/reconciliation.ts`, `firebase-admin`/`resend`/`stripe`/`drizzle-orm` only in route handlers and server libs. Firebase client SDK is dynamically imported at point of use (`user-menu.tsx:17-18`, `auth-callback.tsx:16-17`) so it stays out of shared chunks. Stripe.js loads only on payment routes. `APP_CHANGELOG` (the whole changelog inlined via `next.config.ts` env) is referenced only in the server-rendered `changelog/page.tsx:59`, so it does not ship to the client. Remaining wrinkle: 19 client `page.tsx` files means most admin screens ship their full logic as JS. Assessed, acceptable today; F-4 is the fix path.

12. **Image/asset optimisation.** `next/image` used consistently for logos and icons; all images are local (`public/`, `/tenants/{slug}.{ext}`), so the absence of `remotePatterns` in `next.config.ts` is correct, and Cloud Run standalone output includes sharp. Assessed, no issue with optimisation itself, but where the tenant logo lives is a real problem (F-1).

13. **Rendering strategy.** Mostly right: authenticated pages are dynamic by nature (cookies), and `force-dynamic` is applied where prerendering would mislead (`admin/page.tsx:17`, `sign-in/page.tsx:10`). The exception is the marketing landing page, which is `force-dynamic` plus `revalidate = 0` with two DB round-trips per anonymous hit (`src/app/page.tsx:13-14`, `getLandingContent()` + `getAuthUser()`). See F-11.

14. **Multi-tenant theming/branding.** In-app branding is logo plus name only (`src/components/app-header.tsx:35-42`); tenant colours exist solely in the email pipeline (`src/lib/email-templates.ts`, `email-block-renderer.ts`). The web UI's primary colour is hardcoded (teal `#0d9488` in `payment-step.tsx:156`, oklch teal in the top loader at `layout.tsx:48`). That is an acceptable scope decision for tenant #2 provided you know it; the logo storage mechanics are not (F-1).

15. **Frontend auth integration.** The flow architecture is sound: Firebase client completes the magic link, exchanges the ID token for a server session cookie (`src/app/api/auth/session/route.ts:20-35`), and everything after that is httpOnly-cookie based; no tokens in localStorage (only the pre-auth `emailForSignIn` hint, which is the Firebase-documented pattern). PWA standalone detection routing to OTP, passkey affordance gated on `browserSupportsWebAuthn()` plus a local "prompted" flag, `NotAllowedError` treated as user cancellation not failure (`sign-in-form.tsx:60`): this is thoughtful auth UX code. Two real defects: the unvalidated `redirect` param (F-6) and the in-memory OTP store (F-2), plus missing rate limiting on the send endpoints (F-7).

16. **Frontend test coverage and strategy.** Four vitest files, 892 lines, all pure logic: `permissions.test.ts` (thorough, tenant-isolation cases included), `flow-validation`, `payment-determination`, `workflow-validation`. That is the right 20% to have tested first. But there are zero component tests, zero Testing Library usage, no jsdom environment configured in `vitest.config.ts`, and no e2e harness, for a product whose regressions have historically been UI-workflow-shaped (per the project's own feedback log: double-click approve, missing buttons, drawer scroll-lock). See F-9.

17. **TypeScript rigour.** `strict: true` inherited from the root tsconfig, and most components carry proper prop types. Leakage is concentrated exactly at the server-to-client-props boundary: 26 `: any`/`as any` sites, worst in `admin/requests/[id]/page.tsx` (lines 209, 237, 289, 300, 321, 333, 350-364) where already-typed Drizzle rows are re-mapped through `(al: any)`. See F-5.

18. **Frontend observability.** `sentry.client.config.ts` is sensibly configured (DSN-gated, 0.1 traces, replay on error only, release tagged from the release-please manifest, which is genuinely nice). But there is not a single manual `Sentry.captureException` in app code, no `global-error.tsx` to catch root render errors (the Sentry Next.js SDK explicitly needs one for App Router render crashes), and no web-vitals reporting beyond what the 10% trace sample incidentally captures. See F-3 and F-12.

19. **UX consistency admin vs member.** Strong. Both surfaces share `AppHeader`, the status badge vocabulary (`status-badge.tsx`), the card grammar, and the mobile view-switch that lets admins flip between admin and member views (`app-header.tsx:20-29`). The member dashboard and admin detail pages read as one product. Assessed, no issue.

20. **Dependency health.** Core is current (Next 15.5.x, React 19, Tailwind 4, vitest 4). Three genuine problems: `shadcn` (the CLI) sitting in runtime `dependencies`; `xlsx@0.18.5`, the abandoned npm build of SheetJS with known unpatched advisories (prototype pollution, ReDoS); `@simplewebauthn/*@^11` two majors behind. See F-13.

21. **Stripe Elements integration.** Robust, and unusually so for a solo build. `payment-step.tsx` caches `loadStripe` per connected account (lines 25-39), which is the subtle Stripe Connect requirement most integrations get wrong; it calls `elements.submit()` before `confirmPayment` (the deferred-payment-flow requirement); it handles `onLoadError` with a human message about incomplete Connect onboarding; it degrades gracefully when the publishable key is absent. The `/pay/[id]` page handles the already-paid replay case explicitly. One gap: after a redirect-based payment method returns to `/t/{slug}/dashboard`, nothing inspects `payment_intent_client_secret`/`redirect_status`, so the user gets no success or failure confirmation on return; correctness is preserved by the webhook, so this is UX not money risk. Assessed as a Low; folded into recommendations rather than a numbered finding.

22. **i18n/copy management.** None, and that is fine. Single-market Australian product, `lang="en-AU"` set in the root layout, `en-AU` date formatting via `format-date.ts`. Hardcoded strings are the correct amount of infrastructure for this stage. Explicit pass. The one wrinkle: `Australia/Melbourne` is hardcoded in display formatting (`admin/requests/[id]/page.tsx:237`) while tenants carry a `timezone` column in `src/lib/tenant.ts`; a second tenant in Perth would see wrong dates. Folded into F-14.

## Strengths

Things I would tell you not to touch:

- **S-1: The `withAuth`/`withTenantAuth` wrapper pair (`src/lib/api.ts`).** Every tenant API route gets authentication, tenant resolution, and permission or membership checks through one 113-line, fully typed chokepoint, with server layouts independently re-checking (`admin/layout.tsx:26-29`). This is the single most important pattern in a multi-tenant codebase and it is done right. Defence in depth without ceremony.
- **S-2: The deliberately minimal service worker (`public/sw.js`).** Four lines, install-and-claim only, with a comment stating the decision: no offline caching, the app requires network. Most teams cargo-cult Workbox precaching into an authenticated CRUD app and then spend months debugging stale-HTML sessions. This restraint is distinguished-engineer behaviour. Same for choosing plain `useState` over a state library.
- **S-3: The Stripe Connect handling in `payment-step.tsx`.** The per-connected-account `loadStripe` cache (lines 25-39) is the kind of detail that only exists because someone hit the failure mode and understood it. Combined with `elements.submit()` ordering and the no-key fallback, this is production-grade payments code.
- **S-4: One UI vocabulary, everywhere.** The `components/ui/` kit over `@base-ui/react`, shared skeletons, shared status badges, and the admin/member view-switch produce a product that feels coherent across 33 pages. For a second tenant this consistency is a sales asset.
- **S-5: Battle-scar hardening in the mobile layer.** `mobile-admin-nav.tsx`'s pathname-effect failsafe, `queue-item.tsx`'s stacked tap-target pattern, and the PWA-mode OTP switch in `sign-in-form.tsx` all encode real device-level lessons in code and comments.

## Findings

### [HIGH] F-1: Tenant logo uploads write to the container filesystem and allow SVG
**Evidence:** `src/app/api/v1/t/[slug]/config/logo/route.ts:92-99` writes the uploaded file to `path.join(process.cwd(), "public", "tenants")` and stores `/tenants/{slug}.{ext}` on the tenant row. The app runs on Cloud Run with `output: "standalone"` (`next.config.ts`). `ALLOWED_TYPES` (lines 12-19) includes `image/svg+xml`. SMLSC's logo only survives because `public/tenants/south-melb-lsc.jpg` is committed to the repo.
**Impact:** Cloud Run's filesystem is per-instance and ephemeral. The moment tenant #2 uploads a logo through the UI, it works until the next deploy or instance recycle, then 404s across their app header and every branded page; with more than one instance it is inconsistent immediately. This is a direct second-tenant onboarding blocker dressed up as a working feature. The SVG allowance adds a stored-XSS vector: an admin-uploaded SVG served same-origin from `/tenants/x.svg` executes script when navigated to directly.
**Remediation:** Store logos in a GCS bucket (the infra already lives in GCP) and either serve via public bucket URL with `images.remotePatterns` added to `next.config.ts`, or proxy through a route handler. Drop `image/svg+xml` from `ALLOWED_TYPES`, or if SVG must stay, sanitise server-side and serve with `Content-Disposition: attachment` from a sandboxed path. Small, contained change; do it before tenant #2 touches settings.

### [HIGH] F-2: OTP sign-in depends on a single-instance in-memory Map
**Evidence:** `src/lib/otp-store.ts:1-2`: "In-memory OTP store (production would use Redis)" over a module-level `Map`. This backs `/api/auth/send-otp` and `/api/auth/verify-otp`, which is the only sign-in path for the installed PWA (`sign-in-form.tsx:78-88` routes standalone mode to OTP).
**Impact:** Any Cloud Run scale-out, instance recycle between send and verify, or deploy mid-flow makes valid codes vanish, presenting to members as "Invalid code" with no diagnostic trail. Post cost-optimisation you are likely on min-instances 0 or 1, so cold starts alone can eat codes today. This is intermittent auth failure for the least technical users on the flagship mobile surface, and it will be misfiled as a Firebase bug when it happens.
**Remediation:** No Redis needed. Persist OTPs to a small Postgres table (email, hashed code, expiry, attempt count) via the existing Drizzle setup; delete on verify. Ten lines of schema, one migration, and it also gives you attempt-limiting for free (see F-7). Same argument applies to the WebAuthn challenge store if it uses the same pattern (`src/lib/webauthn.ts` is worth the same check).

### [HIGH] F-3: No error boundaries anywhere, so render crashes are blank screens and invisible to Sentry
**Evidence:** Exhaustive find across `src/app`: zero `error.tsx`, zero `global-error.tsx`, zero `not-found.tsx` files. `sentry.client.config.ts` initialises the SDK, but the Sentry App Router integration cannot capture root render errors without a `global-error.tsx`, and no app code calls `Sentry.captureException` (grep: zero hits outside the config files).
**Impact:** Any thrown render error, including the `(al: any)` mapping code in `admin/requests/[id]/page.tsx` hitting an unexpected shape, gives members and admins Next's unstyled production error page with no recovery affordance, and you may never learn it happened. For a paid product with 192 members this is your single cheapest observability and UX win left on the table.
**Remediation:** Add `src/app/global-error.tsx` (Sentry's documented template, `Sentry.captureException(error)` in a `useEffect`, branded retry button) plus segment `error.tsx` files at `t/[slug]/admin` and `t/[slug]/dashboard` that keep the tenant chrome and offer "Try again". Add a root `not-found.tsx` while there. Half a day, no risk.

### [MEDIUM] F-4: Split-brain data fetching across sibling admin pages
**Evidence:** `admin/page.tsx` (requests queue) and `admin/requests/[id]/page.tsx` are server components querying Drizzle; `admin/members/page.tsx:87-160`, `admin/fobs/page.tsx`, and all `admin/config/*` pages are client components hand-rolling `fetch` + `useState` + debounce + infinite scroll, re-declaring response types locally (`Member`, `Stats` at `members/page.tsx:22-42`) that drift from the route handler's actual output. The project's own backlog item 3 ("requests queue needs refactor to client-side fetching") points the migration in the wrong direction.
**Impact:** Every feature touching a list pays twice: once in the route handler's shape, once in each page's local retyping, with `(m: any)` casts papering over the seam (F-5). New-contributor (or new-agent) cost is high because "how do I load data" has two answers depending on which sibling you copy. Under a second tenant's feature requests this is the main velocity drag.
**Remediation:** Pick one idiom per surface and write it down in the repo. My recommendation: server components remain the default for read views (keep the queue as-is; resist backlog item 3's client refactor and instead add `searchParams`-driven pagination), and client interactivity fetches through a single typed helper in `src/lib` whose response types are exported zod schemas from `packages/shared`, shared by handler and consumer. Migrate opportunistically, members page first since it already has the worst duplication.

### [MEDIUM] F-5: `any` leakage concentrated at the server-to-props boundary
**Evidence:** 26 `: any`/`as any` sites in non-test code. Worst offender is `src/app/t/[slug]/admin/requests/[id]/page.tsx` (lines 209, 237, 289, 300, 321, 333, 350-364) where Drizzle-typed query results are mapped through `(al: any)`, `(f: any)`, `(r: any)` into child props. Client-side equivalents at `components/orphan-linker.tsx:53` and `components/edit-credential-form.tsx:113`. Drizzle write paths use `as any` to defeat the type system (`src/lib/config-crud.ts:71,117,148`, `config/settings/route.ts:76`).
**Impact:** These are exactly the joints where refactors break silently; strict mode is on but neutered at the boundaries that matter. The `config-crud.ts` `as any` casts on `.set()`/`.values()` can hide a real column-name mismatch until runtime in production.
**Remediation:** Type the aggregate query result once (`type RequestDetailData = Awaited<ReturnType<typeof loadRequestDetail>>`) and let inference flow; replace the `config-crud` casts with a generic constrained to the table's `$inferInsert`. Turn on `@typescript-eslint/no-explicit-any` as `error` in `eslint.config.mjs` to hold the line. One focused day.

### [MEDIUM] F-6: Open redirect through the `redirect` query parameter
**Evidence:** `src/app/sign-in/sign-in-form.tsx:22` takes `redirect` from the URL unvalidated and `routeFromResponse` (lines 130-138) falls through to `router.push(redirectTo)`; `src/app/auth/callback/auth-callback.tsx:10,78` does the same with `router.replace(redirectTo)`. Grep confirms no `startsWith("/")` style validation anywhere in the app.
**Impact:** `https://accessbuddy.com.au/sign-in?redirect=https://evil.example` lands the user on an attacker page immediately after a successful, legitimate sign-in, which is the highest-trust moment available for credential or payment phishing against club members. Low exploitation likelihood at current scale, but it is exactly the class of finding a second tenant's security questionnaire asks about.
**Remediation:** One shared helper: accept the value only if it `startsWith("/")` and not `startsWith("//")` and contains no `\`; otherwise fall back to `/`. Apply at both call sites plus `middleware.ts:24` where the param is minted. Under an hour.

### [MEDIUM] F-7: Unauthenticated email-sending auth endpoints have no rate limiting
**Evidence:** A purpose-built limiter exists (`src/lib/rate-limit.ts`, with a documented threat model) but grep shows `checkRateLimit` is called only in `requests/submit/route.ts:64`. `/api/auth/send-otp` and `/api/auth/send-magic-link` send email per POST with no limiter; `verify-otp` imports `getClientIp` for audit only (`verify-otp/route.ts:111`) and does not throttle guesses, and the OTP store (F-2) tracks no attempt count against a 6-digit code with a 5-minute window.
**Impact:** Anyone can burn your Resend quota and spam member inboxes with branded sign-in mail (reputation damage in a club community is real), and 6-digit OTP brute force at 5 minutes per code is thin protection without attempt limits.
**Remediation:** Apply `checkRateLimit` keyed on IP and on email to both send endpoints (the lib's API is already designed for this), and add an attempts column to the F-2 OTP table, invalidating after 5 failures. Half a day combined with F-2.

### [MEDIUM] F-8: The request wizard is a 1,117-line single component with no schema validation
**Evidence:** `src/app/t/[slug]/request/request-form.tsx` (1,117 lines, ~20 `useState` hooks) implements the member-facing multi-step wizard: type selection, lookup, email verification, fob selection, payment, exemption, confirmation. Validation is inline `disabled` gating (lines 519, 566, 1026, 1111); zod is in `package.json` but unused client-side. `admin-actions.tsx` (798 lines) and `config/emails/page.tsx` (479 lines) follow the same trajectory.
**Impact:** This is the most business-critical member flow and the project's own feedback log records it taking "5+ fix rounds". Every new request type or step multiplies interacting state flags. It works today; it is the file most likely to regress under change, and its states are untestable in isolation (feeds F-9).
**Remediation:** Do not rewrite it. Extract each step into its own component with typed props, lift the wizard state into a single discriminated-union reducer (`{ step: "lookup", ... } | { step: "payment", ... }`), and validate step payloads with the same zod schemas the submit route already uses from `packages/shared`. Medium effort, high compounding return.

### [MEDIUM] F-9: Zero UI test coverage despite UI-shaped regression history
**Evidence:** `src/__tests__/` holds four logic suites (892 lines: permissions, flow-validation, payment-determination, workflow-validation), all excellent. `vitest.config.ts` configures no jsdom/browser environment; no Testing Library, no Playwright-equivalent, no e2e anywhere in the repo. Meanwhile the project's own feedback file catalogues regressions that were all interaction-level: double-click approve, drawer scroll-lock, Select values not rendering.
**Impact:** The tested layer (pure permission/workflow logic) is not where this product breaks. Before tenant #2, every admin-workflow change is verified only by manual clicking, and the wizard's step logic (F-8) has no harness at all.
**Remediation:** Two tiers, smallest useful first. (1) Add jsdom + Testing Library to vitest and cover the three highest-risk units: the request wizard's step-advance logic, `queue-filter` grouping, and `mobile-admin-nav` open/close on navigation. (2) One smoke e2e (Playwright or your Interceptor tooling) that signs in via dev-login, walks a request from submit to programmed on a seeded DB, and runs in CI before deploy. Do not aim for coverage numbers; aim for the five flows that page you.

### [MEDIUM] F-10: Async status messages and destructive confirms are inaccessible
**Evidence:** No `aria-live`, `role="alert"`, or programmatic `focus()` exists anywhere in `src` (grep verified). Error/success feedback renders as plain `<p>` swaps (`sign-in-form.tsx:189`, `payment-step.tsx:119-121`, wizard throughout). Destructive admin actions use native `confirm()`/`alert()` at 14 sites (`admin/config/page.tsx:98`, `admin/admins/page.tsx:170`, `members/[id]/archive-button.tsx:20`, `components/inline-action.tsx:33,48`).
**Impact:** Screen-reader users get no announcement when sign-in fails or payment errors; keyboard users lose focus context across wizard steps. Club demographics skew older; this is not theoretical for this product. Native `confirm()` also cannot carry tenant branding and reads as jank inside the installed PWA.
**Remediation:** Wrap the existing error `<p>` pattern in one small `<FormMessage role="alert">` component and adopt it at the ~10 async call sites; move focus to the step heading on wizard step change; replace `confirm()` with the already-built `ui/dialog.tsx` via a reusable `ConfirmDialog`. The primitives all exist; this is assembly, not construction.

### [LOW] F-11: Marketing landing page is force-dynamic with per-hit DB reads
**Evidence:** `src/app/page.tsx:13-14` sets `dynamic = "force-dynamic"` and `revalidate = 0`; every anonymous hit runs `getLandingContent()` (DB) and `getAuthUser()` plus a second `getLandingContent()` in `generateMetadata`.
**Impact:** Slowest possible TTFB on the page whose whole job is first impressions for prospective tenant clubs, plus needless Cloud Run/DB load on the route bots hammer hardest. Contradicts the recent cost-optimisation work.
**Remediation:** The auth check only routes signed-in users away, so move that to `middleware.ts` (cookie presence is already readable there) and give the page `revalidate = 300`. Landing-content edits via `/admin/landing` can `revalidatePath("/")`.

### [LOW] F-12: No web-vitals signal
**Evidence:** `sentry.client.config.ts` has `tracesSampleRate: 0.1` and nothing else measures the client; no `useReportWebVitals`, no vitals beacon.
**Impact:** You shipped a mobile PWA to a member base you cannot observe; INP regressions from the heavy client admin pages (F-4) would be invisible until a human complains.
**Remediation:** Either raise Sentry's sample for pageload transactions or add the one-file `useReportWebVitals` hook posting to a route handler that logs to Cloud Logging. An hour.

### [LOW] F-13: Dependency hygiene, three specific items
**Evidence:** `apps/web/package.json`: `"shadcn": "^4.1.1"` (a code-generator CLI) in runtime `dependencies`; `"xlsx": "^0.18.5"`, the abandoned npm distribution of SheetJS with unpatched public advisories (used server-side in `src/lib/services/reconciliation.ts`); `@simplewebauthn/browser`/`server` pinned `^11` (current major is 13, with API changes in credential verification).
**Impact:** `shadcn` bloats installs and the Docker image for zero runtime value. `xlsx` parses admin-uploaded spreadsheets, which is precisely the input path its ReDoS/prototype-pollution advisories concern. Old simplewebauthn majors will complicate the next passkey-related fix.
**Remediation:** Move `shadcn` to devDependencies or delete it (S). Replace `xlsx` with `exceljs` or consume SheetJS's maintained CDN distribution (M, isolated to reconciliation.ts). Schedule the simplewebauthn v13 bump with a passkey regression pass on a real device (M).

### [LOW] F-14: Tenant timezone is modelled but not honoured in the UI
**Evidence:** `src/lib/tenant.ts` selects a per-tenant `timezone`; display code hardcodes `Australia/Melbourne` (`admin/requests/[id]/page.tsx:237`, and `src/lib/timezone.ts` exists but is bypassed at several call sites).
**Impact:** Invisible with one Melbourne tenant; wrong dates on day one for any tenant outside AEST. Cheap to fix now, annoying to audit later.
**Remediation:** Route all date display through `format-date.ts`/`timezone.ts` taking the tenant's timezone, and grep-ban the literal `Australia/Melbourne` outside that lib.

## Recommendations (ranked)

Ranked by risk reduction per unit effort:

1. **Add `global-error.tsx`, segment `error.tsx`, `not-found.tsx` with Sentry capture (F-3) — S.** Half a day; converts every future unknown crash from silent blank screen into a branded retry plus an alert.
2. **Validate the `redirect` param (F-6) — S.** One helper, three call sites, closes the only exploitable-today frontend finding.
3. **Move OTPs (and attempt counts) to Postgres, and rate-limit the auth send endpoints (F-2, F-7) — S/M.** Removes the single-instance assumption from your primary mobile auth path before growth, not after the incident.
4. **Move tenant logos to GCS and drop SVG uploads (F-1) — M.** The literal second-tenant onboarding blocker; nothing else on this list matters if their logo vanishes in week one.
5. **Fix `xlsx` and `shadcn` dependencies (F-13) — S/M.** Cheap CVE surface removal on an admin upload path.
6. **Write down and converge the data-fetching idiom, typed via shared zod schemas; burn down the boundary `any`s as you go (F-4, F-5) — M.** This is the velocity investment; do it as a standing rule applied to every touched page rather than a big-bang refactor.
7. **Decompose the request wizard into steps with a reducer and schema validation (F-8) — M.** Highest-value refactor once error boundaries and tests exist to catch mistakes.
8. **Add jsdom component tests for wizard/queue/nav plus one CI smoke e2e (F-9) — M/L.** The e2e alone would have caught most of the regressions in your feedback log.

# Backend Review — AccessBuddy (v1.10.2, HEAD 7becae0)

## Assessment (what is built)

AccessBuddy is a Next.js App Router application (`apps/web`) exposing ~84 route handlers under `src/app/api`, backed by Drizzle ORM over Cloud SQL Postgres (`packages/db`) and a shared enum/schema/state-machine package (`packages/shared`). There is no Hono server despite the project description; the API is pure Next.js route handlers. Three auth patterns coexist: wrapper-based (`withAuth`/`withTenantAuth` in `apps/web/src/lib/api.ts`), a workflow-action factory (`apps/web/src/lib/workflow-action.ts`), and manual inline `getAuthUser` + `resolveTenant` + `checkPermission` in the majority of tenant routes.

The domain core is strong: the fob-request lifecycle is an xstate machine (`packages/shared/src/state-machine.ts`) with an authoritative transition guard, driven through a single `transitionRequest` service (`apps/web/src/lib/services/requests.ts`) that owns payment determination, credential allocation, access-level cascade, auto-refund, and email side effects inside one transaction. Tenant isolation is intended to be enforced by Postgres row-level security: `withTenant` (`apps/web/src/lib/with-tenant.ts`) opens a transaction and calls `set_config('app.current_tenant_id', …, true)` (`packages/db/src/rls.ts`), and migration `0001_rls_policies.sql` enables and FORCEs RLS on twelve tenant tables. Firebase Auth (session cookie, WebAuthn, OTP) sits in `apps/web/src/lib/auth.ts`. Stripe Connect (Express) with dual-secret webhook verification handles payments (`apps/web/src/lib/stripe.ts`, `apps/web/src/app/api/webhooks/stripe/route.ts`). Email runs through Resend with per-tenant branding and audit (`apps/web/src/lib/services/email.ts`). A single daily cron (`apps/web/src/app/api/cron/daily/route.ts`) does all scheduled work.

Single live tenant (SMLSC). The system is functional and coherent; the risks below are almost all about the second-tenant transition, which is the stated near-term goal.

## Strengths

1. **The request lifecycle is a real state machine, not ad-hoc status writes.** `packages/shared/src/state-machine.ts` defines transitions declaratively, `getValidEvents` + `validateTransition` (`requests.ts:81`) reject any illegal event from the current state, and every mutating request endpoint funnels through `transitionRequest`. This gives idempotency for free: a double-clicked approve re-issues `APPROVE` from `AWAITING_PROGRAMMING`, which is not a valid from-state, so it throws a 400 rather than double-applying. This is the correct structural fix for the historical double-submit bug class, and it is well tested (`__tests__/flow-validation.test.ts`, `packages/shared/src/__tests__/state-machine.test.ts`).

2. **The email pipeline is disciplined and matches the flagged quality bars.** `setEmailBranding()` is called before rendering (`email.ts:497`, `:996`), every send writes an audit entry carrying `subject` plus explicit `success`/`suppressed`/`noop`/`error` states (`writeEmailAudit`, `email.ts:276-313`), failures never throw into the caller, and daily summaries are de-duplicated with a SHA-256 fingerprint of the visible request IDs (`email.ts:1030-1052`). Audit writes are deliberately threaded through the caller's `tx` so they share the tenant transaction.

3. **The core domain invariant is respected.** Access level lives on `tenantMemberships.accessLevelId`; `transitionRequest` on `APPROVE` sets the level on the membership and cascades a `programmingRequired` flag onto the member's other active credentials (`requests.ts:524-577`) rather than reissuing fobs. Credentials only carry status/expiry/programming state. This is exactly the rule in `feedback_accessbuddy_datamodel.md`.

4. **Config-fragility lessons were partly internalised.** The cron fails closed with a constant-time secret compare when `CRON_SECRET` is missing (`cron/daily/route.ts:14-31`), the Stripe webhook verifies against both connect and platform secrets (`webhooks/stripe/route.ts:29-52`, the documented fix for the missed platform events), TypeScript is `strict`, and env is zod-validated (`apps/web/src/env.ts`).

## Findings

### [Critical] B-1: Tenant isolation depends on RLS that is almost certainly not enforced against the application's DB role, and several queries have no application-layer tenant filter to fall back on

Two facts in the codebase are mutually exclusive unless the app's Postgres role bypasses RLS. `buildAuthContext` (`apps/web/src/lib/auth.ts:189-202`) selects from `tenant_memberships` LEFT JOIN `admin_assignments` on the bare `db` client with **no** `withTenant` and **no** tenant context set. Both tables have `ENABLE` + `FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY` (`packages/db/drizzle/0001_rls_policies.sql:78-79`) with policies of the form `tenant_id = current_setting('app.current_tenant_id', true)::uuid`. With no context set, `current_setting(...,true)` is NULL, `tenant_id = NULL` is never true, so an enforced policy returns **zero rows** — which would make login impossible for every user. Since login works in production, the `accessbuddy` role (`infra/terraform/main.tf:167`) is bypassing RLS (Cloud SQL grants it `cloudsqlsuperuser`; it also owns the tables). The same is true of the cron's bare cross-tenant reads. 

The consequence: RLS is effectively inert for the app connection, so tenant isolation rests entirely on application-layer `eq(table.tenantId, …)` filters and `resolveTenant` + permission checks — **not** on `withTenant`. That matters because code written to trust RLS omits the filter. The clearest example is `createConfigEndpoints` (`apps/web/src/lib/config-crud.ts:36-38`): `withTenant(tenant.id, tx => tx.select().from(table))` with **no where clause**. This factory backs access-levels, credential-types, pickup-locations, and user-group-rules. If RLS is not enforcing, the moment a second tenant exists this returns *every* tenant's configuration. `transitionRequest` similarly fetches the request by `eq(fobRequests.id)` alone (`requests.ts:219-223`) inside `withTenant`, trusting RLS to scope it.

- **Impact:** Cross-tenant configuration and data read/write as soon as tenant two onboards. This is the single largest blocker to a second tenant.
- **Remediation:** (1) Verify empirically with one query — connect as the app role, `SELECT rolbypassrls FROM pg_roles WHERE rolname='accessbuddy'` and `SELECT count(*) FROM credential_types;` with no context set. (2) If it bypasses, either run the app under a dedicated non-owning role with `NOBYPASSRLS` so the FORCE policies actually bite, or (safer and explicit) add `eq(table.tenantId, tenant.id)` filters to every query and treat RLS as defence-in-depth only. Start with `config-crud.ts` and any `tx.select().from(...)` that has no tenant predicate.

### [High] B-2: The WebAuthn/OTP session signing secret has a hardcoded fallback, so a missing CRON_SECRET yields forgeable session cookies

Session cookies for the WebAuthn and OTP paths are HMAC-signed with `process.env.CRON_SECRET ?? "webauthn-session-secret"` (`apps/web/src/lib/auth.ts:76`, mirrored in `apps/web/src/app/api/auth/verify-otp/route.ts:55`). If `CRON_SECRET` is ever unset — precisely the failure mode the project has already hit twice via `gcloud --set-env-vars` wiping the environment (`context/feedback_gcloud_env_vars.md`, `context/state.md` cost-opt notes) — the signing key silently becomes a public constant from the source tree. An attacker can then mint `webauthn.<base64 payload>.<hmac>` for any email and authenticate as any user. Two independent problems compound: the fragile-env history makes "unset" plausible, and reusing the cron secret as the session key means one rotation breaks both surfaces.

- **Impact:** Full account takeover if the env var is wiped or unset; no separation between cron auth and session signing.
- **Remediation:** Introduce a dedicated `SESSION_SIGNING_SECRET` in Secret Manager, fail closed (throw) if absent rather than falling back to a literal, and add it to the Terraform Cloud Run env with `lifecycle.ignore_changes` so a `gcloud` deploy cannot strip it. Move `STRIPE_PLATFORM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` (still a plain env var per `state.md`) at the same time.

### [High] B-3: `email_configurations` schema exists but has no migration, so the template-admin path errors in production

The table is fully defined in `packages/db/src/schema/email-config.ts` and consumed by `apps/web/src/app/api/v1/t/[slug]/emails/route.ts`, but the drizzle migration journal ends at `0009_reconciliations` (`packages/db/drizzle/meta/_journal.json`) and no `CREATE TABLE "email_configurations"` exists in any `.sql` file. Migrations run on container start (`scripts/entrypoint.sh` → `src/migrate.ts`), so prod has no such table. Any code path that reads/writes it throws a Postgres "relation does not exist" error. This matches the known latent item and `state.md` backlog item 1.

- **Impact:** Email template admin and per-tenant recipient overrides are broken in prod; the endpoint 500s.
- **Remediation:** Run `drizzle-kit generate` to emit `0010_email_configurations.sql` (schema is committed, so this is deterministic), review the diff, and let the startup migrator apply it. Verify no other schema files are ahead of the journal — this one slipped because schema and migrations are generated in separate steps with no drift gate.

### [High] B-4: No migration/schema drift gate, and RLS coverage is maintained by a hand-kept allowlist

B-3 is a symptom of a broader gap: nothing in CI compares `packages/db/src/schema/*` against `packages/db/drizzle/*`, so schema-ahead-of-migration drift ships silently. Separately, RLS table coverage is a manually maintained constant (`RLS_TABLES` in `packages/db/src/rls.ts:54-67`); `email_configurations` and the reconciliation tables are not in it, and there is no test asserting that every table with a `tenant_id` column is in the allowlist. Given B-1, this allowlist is currently moot, but it becomes load-bearing the moment RLS is actually enforced.

- **Impact:** Recurrent drift (new tables/columns not migrated or not RLS-covered) that only surfaces as a prod 500.
- **Remediation:** Add a CI step running `drizzle-kit check`/`generate --dry` that fails on uncommitted diff, plus a unit test that reflects over the schema and asserts every `tenant_id`-bearing table appears in `RLS_TABLES`.

### [Medium] B-5: Emails (external HTTP) are sent inside the database transaction, holding a pooled connection open for the network round-trip

`transitionRequest` awaits `sendTransitionEmail` (`requests.ts:960-970`), and every send inside it calls Resend over HTTP (`email.ts:224`) while still inside the `withTenant` transaction — deliberately, so audit writes share the tenant context. The pool is `max: 10` (`packages/db/src/client.ts:28-32`). A single approve can fire a member email plus multiple admin notifications sequentially, each a network call, all holding one of ten connections. Under concurrent admin activity, or if Resend is slow, the pool exhausts and unrelated requests block. Auto-refund also calls the Stripe API inside the transaction (`requests.ts:880`).

- **Impact:** Connection-pool exhaustion and latency spikes under modest concurrency; a slow third party stalls the DB.
- **Remediation:** Collect the intended emails during the transaction (write the audit rows in-tx if context sharing is the goal), commit, then dispatch the external sends after commit — or move sends to a queue. At minimum, cap the number of in-tx sequential sends.

### [Medium] B-6: Missing indexes on the two hottest tables; only `audit_log` and `reconciliations` are indexed

`fob_requests` and `credentials` have primary keys and one unique constraint (`credentials` on tenant+type+serial, `0004`), but **no** secondary indexes (`packages/db/src/schema/requests.ts`, `credentials.ts`). Foreign keys do not create indexes in Postgres. Hot access patterns run unindexed sequential scans: the admin request queue filters `fob_requests` by `(tenant_id, status)`; `transitionRequest` and the cron look up `credentials` by `ownerId`, `requestId`, `serialNumber`, and `status`; and the dispute webhook looks up `fob_requests` by `stripe_payment_intent_id` (`webhooks/stripe/route.ts:148-152`). Fine at 354 credentials; a real problem at multi-tenant scale.

- **Impact:** Table scans that grow linearly with total rows across all tenants.
- **Remediation:** Add indexes on `fob_requests(tenant_id, status)`, `fob_requests(stripe_payment_intent_id)`, `fob_requests(requester_id)`, `credentials(tenant_id, status)`, `credentials(owner_id)`, `credentials(request_id)`, `credentials(serial_number)`.

### [Medium] B-7: Stripe webhook has no event-level idempotency; replay relies solely on the state machine

The handler processes events with no `event.id` dedup table (`webhooks/stripe/route.ts`). For `payment_intent.succeeded` a duplicate delivery is absorbed because `PAYMENT_RECEIVED` is only valid from `AWAITING_PAYMENT` — adequate. But `charge.dispute.created` and `payment_intent.payment_failed` write audit entries with no precondition, so redelivery duplicates them, and `account.updated` is a last-write-wins update. Stripe *will* redeliver.

- **Impact:** Duplicate audit/dispute entries and redundant writes on redelivery; no defence if a future event type is not naturally guarded by the state machine.
- **Remediation:** Add a `processed_webhook_events(event_id primary key, received_at)` table and short-circuit on conflict at the top of the handler.

### [Medium] B-8: Public `payment-info` endpoint returns a Stripe client secret and member name keyed only on a request UUID

`apps/web/src/app/api/v1/t/[slug]/requests/[id]/payment-info/route.ts` has no auth (by design, for the email pay link) and returns the payment client secret plus member name for any request id in the tenant. Security rests entirely on UUID unguessability. Combined with the unauthenticated `members/lookup` and the token-authed attestation routes, the public surface is wider than the wrapper-protected surface suggests.

- **Impact:** Anyone who obtains/guesses a request UUID sees member PII and a payment client secret.
- **Remediation:** Gate the pay link with a short-lived signed token (same HMAC pattern as attestations) rather than the raw request id, and stop returning the member name on the unauthenticated response.

### [Medium] B-9: Rate limiting is per-instance in-memory and absent on the tenant auth + contact routes

`apps/web/src/lib/rate-limit.ts` is explicitly per-instance (documented trade-off), so the effective ceiling is N×limit across Cloud Run instances. More importantly, the top-level `auth/*` routes are rate-limited but the tenant login routes `v1/t/[slug]/auth/{send-code,send-magic-link,verify-code}` and the public `contact` route are not (confirmed in the route sweep). OTP storage is also in-memory (`apps/web/src/lib/otp-store.ts`), so codes are lost on instance recycle and unshared across instances.

- **Impact:** OTP/magic-link email flooding and contact-form spam per tenant; OTP verification flakiness under multi-instance scale.
- **Remediation:** Apply `checkRateLimit` to the tenant auth and contact routes; when a second tenant lands, move the limiter and OTP store to a shared backend (the code already anticipates this — `env.ts` keeps `REDIS_URL` optional).

### [Low] B-10: `resolveTenant` ignores `deletedAt`; auth orphan-linking writes cross-tenant

`tenants` has a `deletedAt` soft-delete column (`packages/db/src/schema/tenants.ts:26`) and `resolveTenant`'s doc comment claims it returns null for deleted tenants, but the query filters on `slug` only (`apps/web/src/lib/tenant.ts:22-34`) — a soft-deleted tenant stays fully reachable. Separately, `getAuthUser` links orphan requests to a user by email across all tenants with no tenant filter (`auth.ts:154-163`); benign today but a cross-tenant write.

- **Impact:** Soft-deleted tenants remain live; minor cross-tenant coupling.
- **Remediation:** Add `isNull(tenants.deletedAt)` to `resolveTenant`; scope the orphan-link update per tenant.

## Recommendations (ranked)

1. **B-1 — Resolve the RLS-enforcement question and add explicit tenant filters where RLS is trusted (config-crud, bare `tx.select().from()`).** Highest risk-reduction; it is the gate to a second tenant. Start with the one verification query, then patch `config-crud.ts`. **(S to verify, M to remediate)**
2. **B-2 — Dedicated fail-closed session-signing secret in Secret Manager; stop the hardcoded fallback.** Removes an account-takeover path tied to a failure mode that has already happened. **(S)**
3. **B-3 / B-4 — Generate the `email_configurations` migration and add a drift + RLS-coverage gate to CI.** Unblocks a shipped-but-broken feature and prevents recurrence. **(S for the migration, M for the gate)**
4. **B-5 — Move external sends (Resend, Stripe refund) out of the DB transaction.** Protects the connection pool before load grows. **(M)**
5. **B-6 — Add the missing `fob_requests` / `credentials` indexes.** Cheap, pays off at multi-tenant scale. **(S)**
6. **B-7 — Webhook idempotency table.** **(S)**
7. **B-8 / B-9 — Token-gate the pay link; extend rate limiting to tenant auth + contact routes.** **(S–M)**
8. **B-10 — `deletedAt` filter and orphan-link scoping.** **(S)**
9. **Testing gap (coverage item 18):** the four test files are all pure-logic unit tests (state machine, permissions, payment determination). There is no integration test that exercises a route end-to-end, no tenant-isolation test, and no webhook test — the two areas (B-1 isolation, B-7 webhook) that would most benefit. Add a DB-backed test that asserts tenant A cannot read tenant B's config. **(M)**

## Maturity Grade

**C+ (solid single-tenant product; not yet second-tenant-ready).**

Justification: the domain modelling is genuinely good — the xstate lifecycle, the access-level-on-membership rule, the audited/branded email pipeline, strict TypeScript, and zod validation on ~86% of body-accepting routes (coverage items 1-3, 14, 16, 20 all pass well). Error handling and response shape are consistent across the wrappers. What holds the grade down is that the headline multi-tenant safety property is unproven and probably not enforced (B-1): the system leans on RLS that the application role appears to bypass, while a meaningful slice of queries omit the application-layer filter that would otherwise cover them. That is acceptable with one tenant and disqualifying for two. Add the config-fragility exposure (B-2), the shipped-but-unmigrated table (B-3), external I/O inside transactions (B-5), and the absent indexes (B-6), and the picture is a well-built application whose data-layer safety and operational hardening have not yet caught up to its feature maturity. Close B-1, B-2, and B-3 and this moves to a B quickly; the code quality to support that is already here.</result>

The parent agent should persist it to `/home/nicholas-wood/Documents/workspace/projects/accessbuddy/artifacts/reviews/2026-07-02-distinguished-review/03-architecture-review.md`. --- # AccessBuddy As-Built Architecture Review - Reviewer: Distinguished Systems Architect (read-only, no production mutation) - Repo: `/home/nicholas-wood/Documents/workspace/projects/accessbuddy/code` @ HEAD `7becae0` - Product state: live v1.10.2, one tenant (SMLSC, 192 members), about to onboard tenant #2 and introduce SaaS pricing - Date: 2026-07-02 ## Assessment AccessBuddy is a single-service, multi-tenant Next.js 15 application on GCP Cloud Run (`australia-southeast1`), backed by one Cloud SQL Postgres 16 instance (`db-f1-micro`), with Firebase Auth, Stripe Connect Express, Resend and Sentry. Tenancy is a shared schema keyed by a `tenant_id` FK on every tenant table, intended to be enforced at two layers: Postgres row level security (RLS) and a membership-scoped application authorisation wrapper. For a solo founder this is a disciplined build: infrastructure is almost entirely in Terraform, deploy auth uses Workload Identity Federation with no long-lived keys, most secrets are in Secret Manager, and the decision history is unusually well documented. The review changes one headline claim the codebase makes about itself. The RLS layer is well designed but, on the evidence, inert in production: the application connects with a database role that bypasses RLS, so tenant isolation currently rests entirely on the application layer. That is the pivotal finding for the 1-to-N jump and is detailed as F1. ### As-built topology ```mermaid flowchart TD User[Member / Admin browser + PWA] -->|HTTPS| LB[Global External ALB
static IP 136.110.185.146
cert accessbuddy-ssl / NEG accessbuddy-neg
NOT in Terraform] LB --> CR[Cloud Run: accessbuddy-production
Next.js 15 + 84 API routes
min 0 / max 10, 1 vCPU / 1Gi] Sched[Cloud Scheduler daily 02:00
x-cron-secret] --> CR CR -->|Direct VPC egress| SQL[(Cloud SQL Postgres 16
db-f1-micro, private IP
daily backup, PITR OFF, role bypasses RLS)] CR --> SM[Secret Manager: stripe / resend / firebase-admin / cron] CR --> GCS[Cloud Storage assets] CR --> FB[Firebase Auth] CR --> Stripe[Stripe Connect Express, dual webhooks] CR --> Resend[Resend, 27 events] CR --> Sentry[Sentry errors only] Integriti[Integriti Inner Range
MANUAL CSV boundary] -.upload.-> CR GH[GitHub Actions: release-please -> ci -> deploy] -->|gcloud run update --image| CR GH --> AR[Artifact Registry] ``` Request path: `accessbuddy.com.au` resolves through a hand-built Global External ALB (Cloud Run custom-domain mapping is unavailable in `australia-southeast1`). Tenant routing is path based under `apps/web/src/app/api/v1/t/[slug]/...`. Every tenant route is wrapped by `withTenantAuth` (`apps/web/src/lib/api.ts:55`), which authenticates via Firebase, resolves the tenant by slug (`apps/web/src/lib/tenant.ts:19`), and checks membership or a required permission (`apps/web/src/lib/permissions.ts:21`). Data access is meant to run inside `withTenant` (`apps/web/src/lib/with-tenant.ts:16`), which opens a transaction and calls `set_config('app.current_tenant_id', ...)` (`packages/db/src/rls.ts:16`). Mandatory areas passing without a material finding: monorepo package boundaries (2), single-service fitness (4), domain data-model soundness (6), integration architecture (7). All others map to findings below. ## Strengths 1. **A coherent, membership-scoped application authorisation layer.** `withTenantAuth` (`apps/web/src/lib/api.ts:55-113`) enforces authentication, tenant resolution, and per-tenant permission or membership before any handler runs. `checkPermission` (`permissions.ts:21-67`) scopes strictly to the caller's membership in the requested `tenantId`, with a clean global-admin path via null-`tenant_id` admin assignments. This is the isolation control actually operating in production and it is well structured and consistently applied across the 55-plus tenant routes. 2. **Clean package boundaries and a well-factored data client.** `apps/web` depends on `@accessbuddy/db` and `@accessbuddy/shared` as packages and never reaches into raw schema files. The RLS primitive is correctly split: `setTenantContext` plus an `RLS_TABLES` allowlist in the db package (`packages/db/src/rls.ts`), ergonomic `withTenant` in the web app. The client is a proxied singleton cached on `globalThis` to survive HMR (`packages/db/src/client.ts:20-44`). 3. **Infrastructure is codified with honest drift management and no long-lived deploy keys.** `infra/terraform/main.tf` covers VPC, Cloud SQL, Artifact Registry with cleanup policies, Cloud Run, Cloud Scheduler, Cloud DNS (SPF/DKIM/DMARC), Secret Manager and the assets bucket. Deploy auth is WIF (`deploy.yml:46-51`), so there are no SA JSON keys in CI. The known CI-versus-Terraform image drift is managed deliberately via `lifecycle.ignore_changes` (`main.tf:421-428`), and cost cuts are documented in-code with restoration pointers rather than silently deleted. ## Findings ### F1. RLS is well designed but inert in production; tenant isolation is application-layer only (Critical) - Evidence, design: `0001_rls_policies.sql:78-89` runs both `ENABLE` and `FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY` on all twelve original tenant tables, with fail-closed policies using `current_setting('app.current_tenant_id', true)::uuid`. On paper this is defence in depth. - Evidence, runtime bypass: the application connects as the table-owning `accessbuddy` user (`main.tf:167-172`; migrations run as the same `DATABASE_URL` user, `packages/db/src/migrate.ts`). The live authentication path performs raw-`db` reads and writes against FORCE-RLS tables with no tenant context set: `getAuthUser` reads `users`, then updates `fob_requests` for orphan linking (`apps/web/src/lib/auth.ts:154-163`) and builds memberships from `tenant_memberships` / `admin_assignments`, all via the raw `db` client (it imports only `@accessbuddy/db`, never `with-tenant`, so it cannot be setting context). The daily cron likewise sweeps `tenant_memberships` across all tenants via raw `db` (`apps/web/src/app/api/cron/daily/route.ts:49-65`). Under enforced FORCE RLS with no context, every one of these would match zero rows and login would be impossible. The app authenticates users and links orphans in production, so the production role is bypassing RLS (Cloud SQL created users carry `cloudsqlsuperuser`; verify the exact attribute). The team explicitly recorded skipping the Cloud SQL RLS smoke test as "not required" (`PATH_TO_PRODUCTION.md:47`), so this was never caught. ISC-18 (fail-closed verified) remains unchecked in the ISA. - Compounding: `0009_reconciliations.sql:15-52` adds `ENABLE` but not `FORCE`, and omits the two tables from `RLS_TABLES`.
